name: Russet Pyre
geological_features: Tidal volcanic activity driven by proximity to a gas giant primary
Lava geysers erupting to heights of several kilometers in low gravity
Surface fractures glowing with subsurface magma
specific_features: Escape pod debris field from an unidentified vessel
description: Russet Pyre is a small, tormented moon orbiting a gas giant, its interior kept molten by tidal forces that flex and compress the rocky body with every orbit. The surface is a patchwork of dark russet stone and glowing fractures, like a coal that refuses to cool, and the low gravity allows lava geysers to erupt to extraordinary heights, their arcs of molten rock tracing slow parabolas against the looming bulk of the parent planet. The gas giant fills a quarter of the sky, its banded clouds reflecting enough light to illuminate even the nightside hemisphere in pale amber tones.

The ground trembles constantly, a vibration felt through the boots that never quite stops, the heartbeat of a world being squeezed to death by its parent's gravity. Lava geysers erupt without warning, sending sprays of molten material across areas that were stable minutes before, and the fracture patterns shift visibly as tidal forces redistribute stress across the surface. In the low gravity, even solid debris launched by eruptions takes long minutes to fall, creating a slow-motion rain of glowing fragments that is both beautiful and lethal.

Scattered across a relatively stable basalt shelf near the northern pole, the wreckage of escape pods from an unidentified vessel tells a story of desperate flight and final failure. The pods date to roughly three decades ago, but no matching ship loss has been recorded in any database, and the pod design does not correspond to any known manufacturer. Personal effects recovered from the least damaged pods suggest the occupants survived initial landing but could not have lasted long in the toxic atmosphere without pressure suits, of which none have been found.

Russet Pyre has no commercial value sufficient to justify the risk of surface operations, but the mystery of the escape pods draws occasional investigators willing to brave the volcanic moon for answers. The tidal volcanic activity is intensifying as orbital mechanics bring the moon fractionally closer to its parent with each passing century, and geological models predict the surface will become entirely molten within a few thousand years. Whatever story the escape pods hold, the pyre is building, and eventually even their metal will be reclaimed by the fire.
